title: Duke’s Laws Marker: Native Rights and Colonial Power
summary: A roadside marker in Hempstead opens a discussion of colonial control over Native land, trade, and religious practice.
address_label: Front Street and Cooper Square East, Hempstead
listing_image_alt: Blue-and-gold Duke’s Laws Convention sign beside a white fence in Hempstead.
ancestral_territory_note: Hempstead was the setting for a colonial code that affected Native communities across the region.
why_this_matters: A roadside sign can celebrate the founding of government while leaving its consequences unstated. Reading the law beside the marker brings Native land rights, religious freedom, and colonial power into the same public history.
introduction_content:
The Duke’s Laws Convention marker stands at Front Street and Cooper Square East in Hempstead. Erected in 1939, the sign commemorates the nearby convention that introduced English colonial law in 1665.

On the Marker

DUKE’S LAWS CONVENTION
HELD NEAR THIS SPOT
IN OLD BUILDING, 1664/5

State Education Department, 1939.
history_title: What the Law Meant for Native People
history_content:
The Historical Society of the New York Courts dates the Hempstead convention to March 1, 1665. Representatives of colonial towns assembled as Governor Richard Nicolls introduced a legal code under English rule.

The code’s section concerning Native people required the governor’s approval for land purchases and licenses for certain trade. It also prohibited Native ceremonial worship, describing it through a hostile Christian framework. These provisions asserted colonial authority over Native economic and spiritual life.

Promises and Restrictions

The same section promised legal redress for injuries and protection for Native cornfields against settlers’ cattle, subject to conditions. These promises sat alongside restrictions on Native trade, land transactions, and ceremonial life.

Read the marker alongside the law itself: a celebration of colonial government also raises questions about whose authority, religious freedom, and land rights that government limited.
whereintheworld_content: The sign stands at Front Street and Cooper Square East, facing Hempstead Town Hall. It can be read from the public sidewalk.
